meta.title: Who really said "It's not the will to win but the will to prepare to win that makes the difference"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Bear Bryant everywhere, but Quote Investigator traces the saying to Michigan coach Fielding H. Yost in 1929–30. No Bryant source exists.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's not the will to win but the will to prepare to win that makes the difference'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bear Bryant. The saying traces to Fielding H. Yost's 1929-30 lectures; the sourced modern version belongs to Bob Knight.

answer.label: Not Bear Bryant — the saying traces to Fielding H. Yost
answer.authorDates: 1871–1946 · University of Michigan football coach & athletic director
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator names Michigan coach Fielding H. Yost as the leading candidate for creating this saying, tracing it to his 1929–30 Wingate Memorial Lectures and a February 1930 address — fifteen years before Bear Bryant became a head coach (Maryland, 1945). The tidy modern wording “it’s not the will to win but the will to prepare to win that makes the difference” is a later compression that no one has tied to any Bryant speech, book, or interview.
answer.confidenceText: The idea is documented from 1929–30 and credited to Yost; the polished sentence attached to Bryant has no primary source.

source.heading: The earliest documented form

docMeta.dd: Intimate Talks by Great Coaches: Wingate Memorial Lectures 1929–1930
Fielding H. Yost, delivered to teachers in New York City

source.excerpt: The will and the wish to win, but there isn’t a chance for either one of them to be gratified or to have any value unless there has been a will to prepare to win.
trail: 1929–30 — Fielding H. Yost tells New York teachers that the wish to win is worthless without “a will to prepare to win,” per Quote Investigator ↗, citing the Wingate Memorial Lectures volume, p. 18.

1965 — Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Vernon Law’s notebook version, in The Pittsburgh Press of 30 July: “Many have the will to win on the day of the contest but few have the will to prepare to win” (QI ↗).
1979 / 2002 — Bob Knight publishes it in a Greensboro Daily News column and later in his memoir; Wikiquote ↗ cites Knight: My Story (2002) for the familiar “everybody has that” form.

Today — close variants of this sentence circulate under Bear Bryant’s name on quote sites such as AZQuotes ↗, which carries “It’s not the will to win that matters—everyone has that” with no publication cited, while Wikiquote’s Bryant page ↗ does not carry it at all.
source.excerptNote: Yost’s phrasing is an argument, not an aphorism — which is why later coaches kept recompressing it. In a separate address, “Lasting Values in Athletics” of 13 February 1930, he put it more plainly: it is “all right to talk about this ‘will to win,’ but I tell you it is not of much worth unless you have the will to prepare.”
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identified first publication, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. The 1929–30 Yost passage shown above comes from a lecture volume whose printing date and edition we have not independently confirmed against a catalogue record, and the closest modern equivalent — Bob Knight’s Knight: My Story (2002) — is firmly in copyright to its authors and publisher.

author.name: Fielding H. Yost
author.kicker: The coach the trail actually leads to
author.heading: Fielding H. Yost
author.bio: Fielding Harris Yost coached Michigan football for 25 seasons between 1901 and 1926 and served as the university’s athletic director from 1921 to 1940. His early “point-a-minute” teams made him one of the most quoted figures in American sport, and he spent his later years on the lecture circuit preaching that athletics built character through preparation, not through wanting to win. That lecture-circuit theme is where the “will to prepare to win” formula first shows up in print.

misattribution.heading: Who really gets credited — and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with at least five claimants and one documented originator. Quote Investigator worked through the chain; Bear Bryant is not in it.

items.why: Quote cards, coaching blogs and aggregators credit Bryant, but none names a speech, book, page or date — and Wikiquote’s Bryant page ↗ lists nothing resembling it in either its sourced or its attributed section.

Quote Investigator ↗ calls Yost “the leading candidate for creator of this saying,” citing his 1929–30 Wingate Memorial Lectures and a February 1930 address in which he said the “will to win” is “not of much worth unless you have the will to prepare.”

Knight used it in a Greensboro Daily News column on 19 December 1979 and published it in his memoir; Wikiquote ↗ cites Knight: My Story (2002) for “The key is not the will to win… everybody has that.”

items.who: Vernon Law, Vince Lombardi, Joe Paterno
items.why: QI ↗ documents Pirates pitcher Vernon Law using a version in 1965, a posthumous 1996 Lombardi credit, and a 1998 attribution to Paterno — all long after Yost.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Yost’s, first documented in 1929–30; the sharpest surviving wording is Bob Knight’s; the Bryant credit is a later, sourceless graft, as Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows.

context.heading: How a lecture-hall point became a locker-room slogan
lead: Yost’s original was not a slogan — it was an argument, delivered to New York teachers, that wanting to win is worthless on its own. His phrasing sprawled: the will and the wish to win have no value “unless there has been a will to prepare to win.” Nobody puts that on a poster.

What happened next is the ordinary life cycle of a coaching maxim. Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Vernon Law wrote his own version in 1965; Bob Knight sharpened it in a 1979 newspaper column and again in his 2002 memoir; it was pinned posthumously on Vince Lombardi and on Joe Paterno. Bear Bryant, the most quotable coach in the American South, simply became the last stop — a name big enough that an unsourced line stops looking unsourced.
context.detailsSummary: Why Bryant is such a magnet for this one
detailsBody: Bryant genuinely did preach preparation, so the sentiment fits him — which is exactly what makes the misattribution durable. A quote that sounds like someone rarely gets challenged.

The wording usually sold as Bryant’s (“It’s not the will to win that matters — everyone has that…”) is close to the version Bob Knight published under his own name in 2002, which is the only form of this saying that carries a real book-and-chapter citation.
context.pull: Yost argued it. Knight sharpened it. Bryant got the credit.
